answers.answer: An HTTP cache stores response bodies and metadata (status and headers) for reuse. The browser private cache serves that user agent; a CDN operates shared edge caches near users; origin is the responsible resource server. A hit reuses a suitable response, while a miss lacks a usable one. Empty caches send browser → CDN → origin and return origin → CDN → browser, storing only where policy permits. A browser hit avoids the network request; another browser that misses locally can get a CDN hit without origin contact. Stored objects are HTTP responses, not replicated database records; hits need not reach origin or its database. CDN request hit ratio is hits divided by requests reaching that CDN: 800/1000 = 80%. The other 200 each make one origin request, so origin receives 200. Browser hits never reach this denominator. Different response sizes prevent interpreting request hits as bytes saved; actual validation, background requests, extra layers and application/database work need separate measurement. Repeated public assets and popular published pages can lower latency through nearby responses and reduce origin request load and transfer. CDN requests/transfer cost money and keys, invalidation and monitoring add work. For low-traffic, mostly private or rarely reused Notes responses, omit shared caching when measured reuse, latency and total-cost benefits do not justify costs; retain privacy rules.

evidence.quote: Our Notes browser requests the public logo with GET. An HTTP cache stores response bodies and metadata, such as status and headers, for reuse. A browser's private cache serves that user agent. A content delivery network (CDN) runs shared caches at edge servers near users. The origin is the server responsible for the resource.

A hit reuses a suitable stored response; a miss lacks one usable for this request. With empty caches, the request goes browser → CDN → origin. The response returns origin → CDN → browser; each cache stores it only if its applicable policy permits.

A browser hit avoids that network request. After another browser misses locally, a CDN hit can return the logo without contacting origin. These are cached HTTP responses, not replicated database records. The origin may read a database, but a cache hit need not reach it.

Request hit ratio is cache hits divided by requests at a specified layer. Here a CDN hit means serving from its cache without contacting origin. Suppose 1,000 GETs reach one CDN after browser caching and 800 are hits. The ratio is 800 / 1,000 = 80%. If each other request makes exactly one origin request, with no extra layers or background requests, origin receives 200.

Browser hits never entered that denominator. Request hit ratio is not byte hit ratio: response sizes differ. Revalidation, background refreshes, extra layers and application work need separate measurements in real traffic; 80% does not prove 80% less database work or transfer.

Repeated public assets and popular published pages can reduce latency by answering nearby, and reduce origin requests and transfer. CDN requests and transfer can incur charges; key configuration, invalidation and monitoring add operational work.

For a low-traffic Notes app serving mostly private or rarely reused responses, omit shared caching if measured benefits do not justify those costs. Compare reuse, latency and total cost. Keep privacy rules intact rather than making private content shared to improve a metric.

answers.answer: Cache-Control carries response caching directives. public explicitly permits shared caching subject to other rules; max-age=60 gives a 60-second freshness lifetime; s-maxage=300 overrides that lifetime in shared caches only. Fresh means young enough for reuse without validation under policy; stale means the freshness limit has been reached, without requiring body deletion. Age estimates seconds since generation or successful origin validation, including cache time. At Age 90 the browser is stale by 30 seconds (60−90=−30; no fresh lifetime remains); CDN is fresh with 300−90=210 seconds remaining. Delivery does not reset age or prove unchanged origin content, and a cache may evict earlier. A representation is the returned resource form, such as HTML. Revalidation checks whether the stored form remains usable. ETag is an opaque representation validator preserved without interpretation. The stale CDN sends conditional GET to origin with If-None-Match: "v1", requesting a body only if the selected representation no longer matches. If unchanged, origin returns 304 without replacement body; CDN updates applicable metadata including freshness and serves its retained body to the ordinary browser GET. If changed, origin returns 200 with new body and ETag: "v2"; CDN serves the new response and replaces its stored representation if policy allows. ETag does not push updates into other caches. 304 saves body transfer on the validation hop, but still contacts origin, which may execute logic or query a database.

evidence.quote: Cache-Control is a response header carrying caching rules called directives. A fresh response is young enough for reuse without validation under its policy. A stale response has reached its freshness limit; its body need not be deleted. Freshness is permission to reuse, not proof that origin content is unchanged.

For a public published Notes page, consider Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300. public explicitly permits shared caching subject to other rules. max-age sets the freshness lifetime in seconds. s-maxage overrides it only in shared caches; the browser still uses 60 seconds.

Age estimates seconds since generation or successful validation at origin, including time spent through caches. If this response arrives with Age: 90, ignoring transit and clock differences, the browser is 30 seconds past its lifetime. The CDN has 300 − 90 = 210 seconds of freshness left. Receiving it does not start a new full lifetime.
A cache may evict a response sooner to free space. Freshness sets reuse limits, not guaranteed retention. When validation is needed, a stored body can still save transfer.

A representation is the returned form of a resource, such as a published note's HTML. Revalidation checks whether the stored representation remains usable. ETag is an opaque validator identifying that representation; clients preserve the tag rather than interpreting it.

The CDN has a stale page with ETag: "v1" and cannot serve it stale under its policy. It sends a conditional GET to origin with If-None-Match: "v1", asking for the body only if the selected representation no longer matches.

If unchanged, origin returns 304 Not Modified without a replacement body. The CDN updates applicable stored metadata, including freshness information, and uses its retained body to answer the browser's ordinary GET.

If changed, origin returns 200 with the new body and its validator, for example ETag: "v2". The CDN replaces its stored representation if policy allows. An ETag does not push changes into other caches.
304 saves retransmitting the body across the validation hop. Origin was still contacted and may run application logic or query a database to decide whether the representation changed.

answers.answer: Cookies are browser-held state: Set-Cookie requests browser storage and Cookie sends state back. Authorization is a request header carrying credentials. Authentication establishes identity; authorization checks permission to read a note. Choose unqualified no-cache for a public page that may be stored but must successfully validate before each reuse. Choose private for a note allowed in browser cache but not shared caches; private does not itself require validation every use, and other directives apply. Choose no-store for sensitive responses HTTP caches must not store. It cannot erase earlier delivered copies or replace access checks. Cookie/Set-Cookie do not automatically partition entries by user or universally prevent caching. Authorization requests have special shared-cache restrictions, but response policy can allow reuse, so authentication does not universally bypass CDN caching. Reusing one user’s response for another can leak private notes. Keep origin authorization and verify explicit private/no-store policy plus actual CDN rules prevent shared storage and reuse on private-note routes. Test different users and do not mark personalized responses public to raise hits.

evidence.quote: Cookies are browser-held state: Set-Cookie asks the browser to store it; Cookie sends it back. Authorization is a request header carrying credentials. Authentication establishes identity; authorization checks permission to read a note.

For a public page, unqualified no-cache allows storage but requires successful validation before every reuse. It does not mean never store. For a private note where browser storage is acceptable, private forbids shared-cache storage; it neither forbids browser storage nor requires validation on every use. Other directives still apply.

For a sensitive note, no-store instructs HTTP caches not to store the response. It cannot erase previously delivered copies or replace permission checks. Choose the policy explicitly instead of relying on a header's misleading name.

A shared response reused for the wrong user can leak private notes. Cookie and Set-Cookie do not automatically create per-user cache entries or universally prevent caching. Authorization-bearing requests have special shared-cache restrictions, but response policy can permit reuse; authentication alone is no universal CDN bypass guarantee.

Keep authorization at origin. For private-note routes, verify that explicit private/no-store policies and actual CDN rules prevent shared storage and reuse. Test different users; do not mark personalized notes public for a higher hit rate.

answers.answer: A cache key identifies the stored response that can satisfy a request. HTTP matching uses method and target URL, with selected headers distinguishing variants, which are different returned forms of the resource. Keep format=pdf and format=html query values distinct and distinguish Accept-Language en and fr. Vary names request headers that must match for reuse; Vary: Accept-Language separates language variants when supported and honored. If CDN ignores query parameters, verify its actual key settings preserve the meaningful format query values as well as language matching; configure correct matching or bypass caching until both survive. Dropping format can return HTML for a PDF request, and dropping language loses the matching language distinction. Irrelevant tracking parameters multiply entries and lower hit rate; exclude them only after confirming they cannot change content. Vary does not modify URLs, grant permission, or override private/no-store; distinct public variants do not authorize sharing private notes.

evidence.quote: A cache key identifies which stored response can satisfy a request. HTTP caching uses the method and target URL, with selected request headers distinguishing variants: different returned forms of the same resource.

Our public Notes export varies by ?format=pdf versus ?format=html, and Accept-Language: en versus fr. Keep the format query values distinct. A CDN configured to ignore them could return HTML for a PDF request; verify the actual key settings rather than assuming every CDN includes every query parameter.

Vary: Accept-Language tells a cache that this request header's value must match for reuse. It separates language variants when supported and honored. CDN support and custom keys differ: verify that both format and language survive the actual matching rules, or bypass caching until they do.

Irrelevant tracking parameters can create extra entries and fewer hits. Exclude them only after confirming they do not change the response. Vary does not change the URL, grant permission or override private/no-store. Correctly separated public variants are not permission to share private notes.

answers.answer: A versioned asset URL changes when its bytes change: publish changed JavaScript as app.v2.js instead of overwriting app.v1.js. Long caching suits immutable bytes at each URL. Update the referring page to request v2; an old cached page can still request v1. For a published page that keeps its URL, choose freshness/revalidation based on acceptable update delay, such as short freshness or validation on every reuse. Editing a database does not rewrite stored HTTP responses. A CDN purge removes or invalidates targeted CDN entries according to provider behavior. Verify relevant URL, variant and CDN-layer coverage, propagation, and completion; do not assume simultaneous replacement. Purging CDN does not evict fresh browser responses or erase downloads. Unpublishing can stop future origin access and trigger purges, but cannot instantly revoke already delivered public content, so choose lifetimes with this limit in mind.

evidence.quote: A versioned asset URL changes when its bytes change: publish app.v2.js instead of overwriting app.v1.js. Long caching fits immutable assets, whose bytes stay unchanged at each URL. Update the referring page to request v2; an old cached page can still ask for v1.

A published note that keeps its URL needs a chosen freshness/revalidation policy matching the tolerated update delay. A database edit does not rewrite stored HTTP responses. Short freshness or validation on each reuse makes a different trade-off from long-lived versioned assets.

A CDN purge removes or invalidates targeted CDN entries according to the provider. Verify coverage of the relevant URLs, variants and CDN cache layers, plus propagation and completion behavior. Purge is an operation to check, not an assumption of simultaneous replacement everywhere.

Purging CDN entries does not evict fresh browser copies or erase downloaded content. Unpublishing can stop future origin access and trigger purges, but already delivered public content cannot be instantly revoked. Choose cache lifetimes with that limit in mind before publishing.

answers.answer: stale-while-revalidate permits bounded stale use while attempting background validation to hide its latency. stale-if-error permits bounded stale fallback on eligible errors such as origin failure. They are optional permissions, not freshness or availability guarantees. max-age=60 makes the page fresh for 60 seconds, with stale allowances counted after expiry. At age 75 it is 15 seconds stale, within the extra 30 seconds allowed through age 90, so serve the stored copy while refreshing in the background. At age 150 it is 90 seconds stale and the eligible error allows fallback within the 120-second stale-if-error allowance through age 180. At age 200 it is 140 seconds stale, beyond both allowances; neither directive authorizes stale reuse even with the error. A cold cache has no response for fallback and exhausted allowances can expose failure. Provider support and policy must permit use; private/no-store are not overridden. Private-note correctness or urgent removal may prohibit showing older content even if fallback helps public-help availability.

evidence.quote: Our public help page tolerates delay. stale-while-revalidate permits bounded stale reuse while attempting background validation, hiding validation latency. stale-if-error permits bounded stale fallback on eligible errors, such as an origin failure. These are optional permissions, not freshness or availability promises.

Consider Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30, stale-if-error=120. Assume cache support, an eligible stored response, no conflicting policy and negligible transit time. The response is fresh for 60 seconds; stale windows start when freshness expires.

At age 75 it is 15 seconds stale: the additional 30-second background-validation window permits reuse while refreshing, through age 90. At age 150 with an eligible error, it is 90 seconds stale: the error allowance lasts another 120 seconds after expiry, through age 180. At age 200 neither extension still permits stale reuse.

A cold cache has no response to fall back to, and exhausted allowances can expose the failure. Verify provider support and policy; these directives do not override private/no-store. Private-note correctness or urgent removal may forbid stale reuse even when it improves public-help availability.
